title: Good Product Strategy, Bad Product Strategy
content:
Once every while, every company will create or review their strategy again. An often taken route is that each department goes out and creates their own strategy: the Technology strategy, the Product strategy, the AI strategy, and the Sales strategy.

Although the main strategy needs to be worked out into actions for each team, this approach often leads to a non-consistent and not-aligned strategy. Each team goes their own way until the next review.

The Rumelt lens

This week I was re-reading the book Good Strategy, Bad Strategy by Richard Rumelt. Although nearly a classic, the basic thoughts are 100% applicable to any product strategy.

Rumelt's central argument is deceptively simple: a good strategy has a kernel made up of three elements:

  1. A diagnosis — defining or explaining the nature of the challenge
  2. A guiding policy — an overall approach to coping with or overcoming the obstacles identified in the diagnosis
  3. Coherent actions — coordinated set of steps, resource commitments, and practical moves that carry out the guiding policy

Bad strategy, by contrast, tends to be characterised by fluff (high-sounding words that say nothing), a failure to face the challenge, mistaking goals for strategy, and listing objectives without any real plan.

Applied to product

Start with the overarching company strategy. If it's solid, work it into plans for different teams — not the other way around. A product strategy that isn't derived from a genuine company-level diagnosis and guiding policy isn't a strategy; it's a wishlist.

A more hands-on guide on how to translate your strategy into a product strategy is written by Shreyas Doshi on Medium.
